jamie: Trying to get a clean nsys + perfetto trace from our model-serving pod to investigate a perf regression. nsys inside the k8s pod fails with permission errors when it tries to mmap perf events. Anyone done this recently?

sara: Yup, did this last week. Two common gotchas: 1) container needs access to the NVIDIA device nodes + uvm, 2) kernel perf settings/sysctls need to allow unprivileged perf.

vikram: For (2) we set kernel.perf_event_paranoid=1 on nodes (or 0 to be more permissive). You can set it via node sysctl or pod securityContext sysctls: 
```
securityContext:
  sysctls:
  - name: kernel.perf_event_paranoid
    value: "1"
```
Note: upgrading to 0 exposes more, but 1 usually works for nsys user traces.

mike: Also make sure the pod has the right device mounts. Example we use in our debug DaemonSet: 
```
volumeMounts:
- mountPath: /dev/nvidia0
  name: nvidia0
- mountPath: /dev/nvidiactl
  name: nvidiactl
- mountPath: /dev/nvidia-uvm
  name: nvidia-uvm
```
and volumes are hostPath to those nodes' devices. If you use the nvidia-container-toolkit runtime that usually wires this up for you.

jamie: I tried with the toolkit + sidecar image "nvcr.io/nvidia/nsight-systems:latest" but the profiler still aborted: "Unable to open /proc/sys/kernel/perf_event_paranoid (Permission denied)". The pod is not privileged.

sara: If you can't change node sysctl, you can run a privileged debug pod on the node to change it temporarily: `kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=alpine --privileged -- sh` then `echo 1 > /proc/sys/kernel/perf_event_paranoid`. Not ideal for prod.

vikram: Another option: use the DaemonSet approach — run an nsight collector as a privileged DaemonSet that collects traces and writes them to a PVC. The collector touches node-level perf APIs so it can capture kernel timelines even for unprivileged app pods.

mike: A few more tips from the last investigation: 
- nvprof is deprecated; use nsys. 
- add `--trace=nvtx,cuda,osrt` to see kernel timelines + OS thread info. 
- short capture windows (2-5s) reduce tracer overhead and make it easier to correlate with request IDs.

jamie: Good call. We're specifically chasing a regression where kernel selection seems to flip from the optimized fused kernel to a slower per-layer kernel under load. We suspect KV cache behavior + batching heuristics cause different kernel launch patterns. Any ideas how to confirm? :thinking:

sara: Capture nvtx ranges around the model inference code and also instrument our batching layer to emit NVTX pushes per-batch. Then in the nsys timeline you can see kernel start/end and whether kernels are fused or many small launches. That will highlight when batching causes more kernel launches (higher kernel launch overhead).

mike: Also profile memory copies and PCIe stalls — sometimes what looks like a kernel regression is actually DMA contention or cache-miss storms from KV cache thrashing. In nsys look at 'CUDA API' vs 'CUDA Kernel' lanes and the memcpy lanes on the timeline.

vikram: We found one real issue: when batch size crosses a quantization boundary, the runtime switches kernel variant that disables a fused path and ends up launching ~3x more kernels. The fix was a small change in kernel selection heuristic to prefer fused codepath for sizes >= N. After the patch, traces showed a single large kernel instead of many small launches and latency dropped.

jamie: Nice. For capturing traces from within a pod without changing node sysctls, can we run nsys in hostPID or with CAP_PERFMON? What capability is required?

ops-bot: Info: modern kernels use CAP_PERFMON for perf_event access; older systems relied on perf_event_paranoid. Kubernetes does not yet have native CAP_PERFMON support in many clusters.

sara: Right — CAP_PERFMON would be ideal but not widely available. So either change the node sysctl, run privileged collector, or run the tracer on the host and point it at the container's PID namespace with `nsys profile --pid <pid>` via `nsenter` / `kubectl debug`.

jamie: Command I'm going to try (short 3s capture): 
```
kubectl exec -it $(kubectl get pod -l app=runtime-debug -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -- \
  nsys profile --output=/tmp/jtrace.nsys --trace=nvtx,cuda,osrt --duration=3 --sample=cpu --file-size=0 --capture-range=nvtx
afterwards: nsys stats /tmp/jtrace.nsys
```

mike: If that chokes on perf_event_paranoid you can instead: 
- schedule a privileged DaemonSet on that node that runs `nsys` and binds mount the target pod's /proc by mounting the container runtime directory, then use `nsys --pid <targetpid>`.

jamie: Thanks all — I'll try the privileged collector variant first (we have a debug NS), run a 3s trace with NVTX around the batching + kv cache lookup, and upload the .nsys file to the ticket. If I see a lot of small kernels and high memcpy activity, I'll open a rollback for the kernel-selection patch and try the old heuristic for comparison. :thumbsup:

sara: Ping me once you have the trace. I can run the perfetto visualization and mark hotspots. :eyes:

vikram: Also add the pod's CPU/memory and GPU utilization metrics for the 30s window around the trace — sometimes scheduler jitter causes batching delays that look like kernel regressions.

jamie: Will do. Logging ticket: https://redwood.internal/tickets/452 (will attach trace).

mike: Awesome. One more reminder: if you need to change file permissions for the nsys binary inside our immutable image, chmod +x might be necessary when we mount it from a debug volume.

jamie: noted. thanks everyone :rocket:
